European brook lamprey larvae hatch at 14 days [ab = 14 days] when incubated at 11 °C [T = 11 °C]. At this point of first exogenous feeding, the young ammocoete possesses a total body length of 2.5 cm [Lb = 2.5 cm] and a very modest dry weight of 0.0052 grams . These early-life metrics, recorded during laboratory rearing trials, reflect the extremely altricial state of the newly hatched lamprey, which relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves prior to burrowing into fine sediment to commence filter feeding. The protracted incubation period underscores the sensitivity of early embryonic stages to ambient temperature within this species' natal streams.

As the ammocoete progresses through its multi-year larval phase, it accumulates substantial somatic tissue before undergoing the radical metamorphic transformation into the juvenile stage. The ultimate dry weight attained by a fully grown adult prior to spawning has been measured at 1.42 grams , corresponding to a maximum total length of 20.0 cm [Li = 20.0 cm], which represents the species' asymptotic body size under typical stream conditions in northwestern Europe. Field surveys of reproductively active adults indicate that individuals achieve this considerable mass only after an extended period of somatic investment, a pattern consistent with other members of the Petromyzontidae. The large difference between hatchling and adult mass highlights the substantial energetic commitment required during the trophic switch from filter-feeding larva to parasitic or non-parasitic juvenile, depending on local population ecology.

The onset of sexual maturation, signaled by the first reproduction event, occurs considerably later in the lifespan of Lampetra planeri. Controlled experiments conducted at a water temperature of 11 °C [T = 11 °C] have demonstrated that individuals attain the capacity for first spawning at 2372 days after hatching [tR = 2372 days after hatching], a duration that encompasses the entire larval, metamorphic, and pre-reproductive adult phases. Coincident with this reproductive milestone, the body length at puberty has been recorded at 12.5 cm [Lp = 12.5 cm]. This substantial delay in breeding, representing more than six years of development, is among the lengthiest pre-reproductive periods documented for any non-migratory freshwater fish of comparable body size. The dry weight at puberty averages 0.38 grams , indicating that a significant fraction of adult mass is accumulated after reproductive maturation begins.

Fecundity estimates for a single spawning event reveal that a female nearing the end of her life produces approximately 1500 eggs per spawning bout  when maintained at 11 °C [T = 11 °C]. This clutch size is moderate relative to other lamprey species, reflecting the trade-off between egg size and number typical of lithophilic spawners. Mature females are entirely semelparous, investing all available energy reserves into a single, catastrophic reproductive effort before somatic death ensues. The modest neonatal length of 2.5 cm [Lb = 2.5 cm] and the hatchling dry weight of 0.0052 grams  stand in sharp contrast to the substantial reproductive output, emphasizing that each offspring represents a minute fraction of the maternal investment, despite the considerable adult body size attained over the long larval period.

Longevity records for Lampetra planeri, though limited by the difficulty of tracking individuals across their entire life cycle, suggest a maximum lifespan of 2555 days [am = 2555 days] based on mark-recapture studies in a German stream system, where annual water temperatures average approximately 8 °C [T = 8 °C]. This seven-year lifespan, while not extreme among lampreys, is notable given the species' small adult body length of up to 20.0 cm [Li = up to 20.0 cm] and its low metabolic rate as a non-feeding adult. The age at first reproduction of 2372 days after hatching [tR = 2372 days after hatching] leaves only a brief window for a single spawning event before physiological death intervenes, reinforcing the species' highly synchronized semelparous life history at a temperature of 11 °C [T = 11 °C]. The entire developmental trajectory, from the 14-day embryonation period (14 days) [ab = 14 days] through to senescence, is tightly constrained by local thermal regimes, making the brook lamprey an excellent model for studying temperature-dependent life-history evolution in freshwater ecosystems at a temperature of 11 °C [T = 11 °C].
